title: My family: who lives with us, and how we know each other

summary.text: With your eyes shut, can you find your mother or your grandmother just by sniffing a shirt she wore? You may find at least one person. Every person has their own smell, and much of it is made by tiny living beings on their skin. People who live together pass these tiny beings to each other. In this unit your child sniffs family shirts in a fair test, passes a smell down a line of hands, and meets families of many kinds, in people and other animals.
summary.art: A girl with a soft cotton dupatta tied over her eyes, sniffing a folded T-shirt inside a steel tumbler that her grandmother holds up to her nose, while her mother and little brother watch and smile.

intro.hook: Close your eyes. Someone in your family hugs you. Can you tell who it is without looking?
intro.text: You know your family by their faces and their voices. Your nose knows them too. Every person has their own smell. In this unit you find out if you can tell your family apart by smell alone. You also meet many kinds of families, in people and in other animals.
intro.art: A small boy with his eyes squeezed shut being hugged from behind by his grandmother in a cotton saree, his face breaking into a smile.

outcomes: By the end I can say who is in my family and who looks after me.
By the end I can name some different kinds of families, in people and in other animals.
By the end I can find some of my family by smell alone, in a fair test.
By the end I can say that tiny living beings called microbes live on our skin, and pass between people who live together.
By the end I can say why we cover our eyes and try twice to make a test fair.

terms.meaning: A family is a group of people who belong to each other and look after each other.
terms.example: Nila's family is her Amma, her Appa, her Ammachi and her little brother Arjun.
terms.art: A family of four sitting on a mat on the floor, eating dosa together from steel plates.

terms.meaning: A relative is someone in your family, near or far, like a grandmother, an aunt or a cousin.
terms.example: Revathi Kunjamma lives in Chennai, far from Nila. She is still Nila's relative.
terms.art: A family photo on a phone screen, with a grandmother, an aunt and three cousins smiling together.

terms.meaning: To adopt a child is to take them into your family as your own son or daughter, for always.
terms.example: Revathi adopted baby Kayal. Kayal is Revathi's daughter now, for her whole life.
terms.art: A woman holding a baby girl close against her shoulder and smiling, with a cradle beside them.

terms.meaning: Smell is the sense that tells you what is in the air, through your nose.
terms.example: You smell sambar before you see the pot, because a little of it floats into your nose.
terms.art: A girl sniffing the steam rising from a pot of sambar on a kitchen stove.

terms.meaning: Microbes are tiny living beings, far too small to see. Some of them live on your skin.
terms.example: Millions of microbes live on your hands right now. Most of them are friendly.
terms.art: A child's open hand, with a round zoom-in bubble showing many tiny round and rod-shaped microbes, drawn bright and friendly.

explanations.definition: A family is a group of people who belong to each other and look after each other.
explanations.description: Every child grows up with someone who feeds them, holds them and keeps them safe. Those people are the child's family. Some people join a family by birth, some by marriage, like a husband and wife, and some by adoption, like baby Kayal. People do not all agree on who counts as family.
examples: Nila lives with her Amma, her Appa, her Ammachi and her brother Arjun in a flat in Kochi.
Farzana lives with her Ammi and her Nani in Hyderabad. Her Abba works in Dubai and calls every night.
Kayal was adopted by Revathi in Chennai when she was a baby. Revathi is her mother.

perspectives.explanation: Family means the people you are related to, by birth, by marriage or by adoption. Cousins in another country are family, even if you have never met them.
Family means the people who live with you and look after you. A neighbour aunty who cares for you every day can feel like family.

explanations.art: Three small family pictures side by side: a grandmother, a mother and a girl in a Kochi flat; a mother, a grandmother and a girl in Hyderabad; a woman holding a baby in Chennai.

explanations.definition: Families can be big or small, and can be made in different ways. Each kind is a real family.
explanations.description: Some families are small, with one parent and one child. Some are big joint families, with grandparents, uncles, aunts and cousins in one house. Some children are raised by a grandmother or an aunt. Other animals have families too. In an elephant family, mothers, daughters, aunts and young ones stay together, and an older female often leads. Grown-up males leave. In an ant nest, a queen lays the eggs, and the ants you see are her daughters.
examples: Meenakshi's joint family in Madurai: Paati, Thatha, Amma, Appa, Periyamma, Periyappa, Meenakshi and two cousins, all in one house.
Joyita in Kolkata lives with her Baba. It is just the two of them, and her Dida visits on Sundays.
The ants on your kitchen floor are all girls. They are daughters of a queen who lives in the nest.
explanations.art: A row of family pictures: a big joint family on a veranda, a father and daughter cooking fish curry, an elephant family walking with an old female in front, and a line of ant sisters carrying a crumb.

explanations.concept: How we know our family by smell
explanations.definition: Every person has a body smell of their own. People can learn the smells of the people they live with, and know them again.
explanations.description: Every person has their own smell. You notice it when you hug someone, or hold something they wore. Scientists have tested this. Brothers, sisters and mothers can pick out a family member's worn T-shirt by smell alone. A new mother can learn her baby's smell in less than an hour. Other animals do this too. A mother sheep smells her new lamb and remembers that smell.
examples: Some children feel calm with Amma's old saree or dupatta, because it smells of her.
A dog greets each person at the door by sniffing them first.
Two ants meet on the wall and touch feelers for a moment, then walk on.
explanations.art: A small girl asleep, hugging a folded old cotton saree printed with small flowers, with a night lamp glowing beside her.

explanations.concept: The tiny living beings we share
explanations.description: Your skin is home to millions of microbes, tiny living beings too small to see. They feed on your sweat, and as they feed they make much of your smell. People who live together hug, hold hands and touch the same things, so they pass microbes to each other. In 2013, scientists in the United States found that people in one home share more skin microbes than people in different homes. Scientists do not yet know if shared microbes stay for long, or come and go after each touch.
examples: Nila's grandmother, Ammachi, hugs Nila's little brother Arjun every morning. Each hug passes a few microbes between them.
Everyone at home drinks from the same steel tumblers and sits on the same sofa.
If the family has a pet dog, she licks everyone's hands and shares microbes with the whole family.

perspectives.explanation: People who live together share more skin microbes than people who live apart, so living together shapes the tiny beings on us.
Some shared microbes may only be passed on for a short time after a touch, and then go away. We need more tests to know which ones stay.

explanations.art: A grandmother and a boy hugging, with a soft glowing cloud of tiny friendly microbes passing between their cheeks and hands.

agreed.text: People can know their family members by smell alone.
agreed.evidence: In 1981, Richard Porter and John Moore in the United States found that brothers, sisters and mothers could pick out a family member's worn T-shirt by smell. Many tests since then have found the same.
agreed.context: This card is about what scientists agree on: our noses can know our family.

agreed.text: Much of a person's body smell is made by microbes on the skin.
agreed.evidence: Fresh sweat has very little smell. The smell comes when skin microbes feed on the sweat. Scientists have found that the smell begins when the microbes break the sweat down.
agreed.context: This card is about what scientists agree on: tiny living beings on our skin make much of our smell.

agreed.text: Families come in many kinds, and every kind can give a child love and care.
agreed.evidence: Children grow up well in big families, small families, with one parent, with grandparents and with adopted parents. What matters most is having grown-ups who care for them every day.
agreed.context: This card is about what is agreed about families: there are many good kinds.

challenging.claim: Humans have a weak sense of smell. Only dogs and other animals really use their noses.
challenging.who: A French doctor, Paul Broca, in 1879, and most people for over 100 years after him
challenging.for: A dog's nose is much better than ours at many smells. The smell part of the human brain is small next to the rest of the brain.
challenging.against: When scientists tested real people, they found humans can tell their own family by smell. Humans have about 400 kinds of smell sensors in the nose. In 2017, the brain scientist John McGann wrote that the weak human nose is a myth.
challenging.context: This card is about an old idea: that people have a poor sense of smell.

challenging.claim: A child who was adopted is not a real part of the family.
challenging.who: An old idea some people still hold
challenging.for: An adopted child was not born to the parents.
challenging.against: Adoption law in India says an adopted child is the child of the adoptive parents in every way. An adopted child is fed, held and loved like any other child. People who live together even share the same skin microbes.
challenging.context: This card is about an old idea: that only children born into a family are real family.

challenging.claim: Your body smell comes from the family you are born into.
challenging.for: Identical twins smell more alike than other brothers and sisters. So genes play a part in body smell.
challenging.against: Food, soap, sweat and skin microbes change body smell too. People who live together, related or not, share skin microbes. How much smell comes from genes and how much from living together is still being studied.
challenging.context: This card is about a question scientists still argue about: where does body smell come from?

big_questions.q: If your smell is made partly by tiny living beings on your skin, is your smell really yours?
big_questions.hint: Think about the microbes on you, and who passed them to you.

big_questions.q: Who is in your family? Is it the people who live with you, or the people you are related to, or both?
big_questions.hint: Think of someone who lives far away, and someone who is not related but looks after you.

big_questions.q: An ant nest can have thousands of ants, all daughters of a queen. What would it be like to have a thousand sisters?
big_questions.hint: Think about who would cook, who would play, and how you would know them all.

big_questions.q: A baby knows their family before they can see clearly or talk. How do you think a baby knows?
big_questions.hint: Think about smell, touch, warmth and voices.

story.title: Ammachi's Shawl
story.note: Nila, Arjun, Amma, Ammachi, Revathi and Kayal are made up. People really can know their family by smell, and people who live together really do share skin microbes.
text: Nila lived in a flat in Kochi with her Amma, her Appa, her little brother Arjun and her Ammachi, her grandmother. Nila was six. Arjun was four.
Every morning, Ammachi oiled Nila's hair with coconut oil and plaited it. Every night, she told a story. Her old cotton shawl lay over her shoulders, soft and faded, with a green border.
One day a phone call came from Chennai. It was Revathi Kunjamma, Amma's younger sister. 'Our baby is home!' she said. Revathi Kunjamma had adopted a baby girl. Her name was Kayal.
'A new baby needs many hands,' said Ammachi. 'I will go to Chennai for two weeks to help.' Nila's face fell. Two weeks felt like forever.
On the night before she left, Ammachi put her shawl round Nila. 'Keep this for me,' she said. 'I will come back for it.'
Nila pressed her face into the shawl. It smelled of coconut oil, of the kitchen, and of Ammachi. She slept at once.
Every evening, Amma phoned Chennai so Nila could say hello to Ammachi. Baby Kayal cried loudly in the background, and Arjun giggled at the noise.

In the first few days the flat felt too quiet. Nila missed the coconut oil and the stories at night. Amma plaited her hair instead, but the plait came out lopsided. Nila laughed, and Amma laughed too. Still, every morning, Nila's first thought was of Ammachi.
Every night, Nila slept with the shawl. Arjun wanted a sniff too. 'It smells like Ammachi!' he said. 'How does a shawl smell like a person?'

Amma was folding clothes. 'Every person has their own smell,' she said. 'You know Ammachi's smell because you are close to her every day. Your nose remembers it.' She sniffed the top of Arjun's head. 'You smell like Arjun,' she said, and he giggled.
At last Ammachi came home, with banana chips and a phone full of photos of baby Kayal. Nila and Arjun hugged her very hard.
Nila gave back the shawl. Ammachi held it to her nose and laughed. 'Ayyo! This smells of you now, Nila, not of me!'

'Your skin is home to tiny living beings called microbes,' said Ammachi. 'They are far too small to see. They make much of our smell. When you hold something close, some of them move onto it. When people hug, some move across too. People who live together pass them to each other all the time.'
'What about baby Kayal?' asked Arjun. 'She was not born in Revathi Kunjamma's family.'

Ammachi showed them a photo. Revathi Kunjamma held Kayal close, cheek to cheek. 'Revathi holds her all day, and they sleep side by side. They are sharing their tiny beings, just like we do. Kayal is her daughter.'
Nila wrapped the shawl round Ammachi's shoulders and hugged her, shawl and all. 'Now it will smell of both of us,' said Nila.
story.epiphany: A family's smell is made by living close together. Kayal shares it too, though she was adopted.
ask: Why did the shawl smell of Ammachi at first, and of Nila later?
Baby Kayal was adopted. How does she come to share her family's smell?
Is there something at home that smells of someone you love? Who is it?
art: A grandmother in a cotton saree plaiting a girl's oiled hair in a sunny Kochi flat, a green-bordered shawl over her shoulders.
A girl asleep in bed, her face pressed into a faded green-bordered shawl, a little boy peeping at her from the door.
A grandmother laughing and sniffing a shawl at the front door, with a bag of banana chips, while two children hug her legs.
A phone screen showing a woman holding a baby girl cheek to cheek, with two children leaning in to look.

games.title: Family Line-Up: who comes first?
games.players: The whole family, 2 or more people
games.context: This is a moving game for the whole family. A caller turns over a card, a grown-up reads it out, and everyone lines up in that order. Is the oldest person always the tallest? Who wakes first? The lines come out different every time.

items.f: Line up from youngest to oldest.
items.b: Ask each person how old they are, if you do not know.

items.f: Line up from shortest to tallest.
items.b: Stand back to back to check.

items.f: Line up by who woke up first this morning.
items.b: The first one awake goes at the front.

items.f: Line up from the smallest hand to the biggest hand.
Line up by who has the longest hair.
items.b: Shortest hair at the front, longest at the back.

items.f: Line up by who has lived in this home the longest.
items.b: The person who came first goes at the front.

items.f: Line up from the smallest foot to the biggest foot.
items.b: Stand side by side and look down.

items.f: Line up by who fell asleep first last night.
items.b: The first one asleep goes at the front.

items.f: Line up from the softest voice to the loudest voice.
items.b: Everyone says 'hello' one at a time.

items.f: Line up by whose name has the most letters.
items.b: Count the letters in each name.

printables.title: Line-up record: 5 lines
items: Line 1: the card was ____________. Draw the stick people in the order they stood.
Line 2: the card was ____________. Draw the stick people in the order they stood.
Line 3: the card was ____________. Draw the stick people in the order they stood.
Line 4: the card was ____________. Draw the stick people in the order they stood.
Line 5: the card was ____________. Draw the stick people in the order they stood.

rules: Cut out the 10 cards. Shuffle them and put them face down. Everyone is on the same team: the goal is to make each line together.
The youngest player is the first caller. The caller turns over a card. A grown-up reads it out.
Everyone lines up in that order. Talk, check and swap places until everyone agrees. If two people tie, they stand side by side.
The caller draws the line on the record sheet as stick people. With two players, the line has two people, and that is fine.
The person at the front of the line is the next caller.
After 5 cards, look at the record sheet. Is the line the same every time? The game ends there.

setup.art: Ten small paper cards face down on a floor mat, with a girl turning one over.
setup.caption: 1. Shuffle the cards. Turn one over and read it.

setup.art: A family of five standing in a line in a living room, shortest at one end, a grandmother in the middle, a tall father at the far end.
setup.caption: 2. Everyone lines up in that order.

setup.art: A record sheet with three rows of stick people, the order of the people different in each row.
setup.caption: 3. Draw the line as stick people. Compare the lines.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the cards. 2. Gather everyone who is at home in the biggest room. 3. Put the cards face down.
flow.say: Today the whole family plays a lining-up game. Do you think the youngest person will always be at the front? Why?
flow.kid: Everyone lines up in a different order each time. Guess who will be first.

ask.q: Will the oldest person always be the tallest?
good: Yes, grown-ups are tall.
No, a grandparent can be shorter than a parent.

flow.parent: Any guess is fine. Write it down. Many children guess that oldest and tallest are the same.

flow.do: 1. Your child turns over the first card and you read it aloud. 2. Everyone lines up. 3. If you are only two, stand in a line of two.
flow.say: Line up from youngest to oldest. Who goes at the front? Who goes at the back?
flow.kid: Line up from youngest to oldest. Where do you stand?
flow.parent: Let your child do the sorting. Help only with ages if needed.

flow.do: 1. Play three more cards. 2. After each line, your child draws it as stick people on the record sheet.
flow.say: Now line up from shortest to tallest. Is the line the same as before, or did someone move?
flow.kid: Now line up by height. Did someone move?

ask.q: Who moved when we lined up by height instead of age?
good: Somebody moved, because the oldest is not always the tallest.
The person at the front changed.

flow.do: 1. Play one card that is not about bodies, like who woke first. 2. Draw that line too.
flow.say: Who woke up first this morning? Line up! Is this line like the others?
flow.kid: Who woke up first today? Line up!

flow.do: 1. Lay the record sheet on the floor. 2. Look at all the lines together.
flow.say: Look at all our lines. Is the same person always at the front? What does that tell us about our family?
flow.kid: Look at all the lines. Is anyone always first?

ask.q: Why are the lines different?
good: Each line sorts by a different thing.
The oldest is not always the tallest.

flow.parent: The point is that every person in a family is first at something. Sorting by different features gives different orders.

check.q: The oldest person is at the back when we line up by age. Is the oldest person always at the back of the line?
options: No, it depends on what we line up by
check.why: The oldest person is at the back when we line up by age. But when we line up by height or by who woke first, they may be somewhere else. Each line sorts by one thing.

experiments.title: Whose Cloth Is This? Can you find your family by smell alone?
experiments.context: In this experiment, everyone at home sleeps one night in a cotton T-shirt or vest. In the morning, each one goes into a steel tumbler. With your eyes covered, you sniff each tumbler and guess whose shirt it is.
experiments.question: Can I tell who wore a shirt just by smelling it, with my eyes covered?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Whose shirt will you know most easily by smell? Whose will be hardest? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Every shirt goes in the same kind of steel tumbler, so the tumblers give no clue. Your eyes are covered, so you cannot see the shirt. Your hands stay in your lap, so your fingers give no clue. Nobody wears perfume the night before. We add one clean, washed shirt, to see what 'nobody' smells like. We do two rounds, because one right guess could be luck.

materials.item: one cotton T-shirt, banian or nightie for each person at home, worn for one night (not freshly washed after)
one clean, washed cotton T-shirt that nobody has worn
steel tumblers or steel dabbas, all the same kind
a dupatta or soft cloth to cover the eyes
small paper chits and a pencil
paper and crayons for the results

schedule.what: In the evening: everyone puts on a cotton shirt or vest for bed. No perfume, no new soap.
In the morning: put each shirt in a tumbler. Cover the eyes, sniff, guess. Do two rounds and record.

experiments.record: Draw one tumbler for each shirt. Under each, draw the face of the person you guessed. Put a tick when you were right.

setup.art: A family of four getting ready for bed in plain cotton T-shirts and vests, a girl pulling hers over her head.
setup.caption: 1. The night before, everyone sleeps in a cotton shirt.

setup.art: A row of identical steel tumblers on a kitchen counter, each with a folded T-shirt stuffed inside, and a small paper chit tucked underneath each one.
setup.caption: 2. In the morning, put each shirt in a tumbler. Hide a name chit underneath.

setup.art: A girl with a dupatta tied over her eyes, sniffing a steel tumbler held under her nose by her mother.
setup.caption: 3. Cover your eyes. Sniff each tumbler and guess whose shirt it is.

flow.do: 1. In the evening, tell everyone about the test. 2. Each person puts on a cotton T-shirt, vest or nightie for bed. 3. Ask everyone not to use perfume or scented powder tonight.
flow.say: Tomorrow we test your nose. Everyone sleeps in a cotton shirt tonight. Whose shirt do you think you will know best? Why?
flow.kid: Everyone wears a cotton shirt to bed tonight. Tomorrow we sniff them. Whose shirt will you know best? Why?

ask.q: Whose shirt will be easiest to know by smell?
good: The person I hug the most.
The person whose hair oil I know.

flow.parent: Write down the guess and the reason. Say nothing yet. Children often guess the person they hug most.

flow.do: 1. In the morning, while your child waits in another room, each person folds their shirt into a steel tumbler. 2. Fold one clean, washed shirt into a tumbler too. 3. Write each name on a chit and tuck it under that tumbler. 4. Mix up the tumblers on the counter.
flow.say: Wait here. We are hiding the shirts in the tumblers. No peeping!
flow.kid: Wait in the other room. No peeping!
flow.parent: All the tumblers should look the same. If some shirts are a different colour, push them right down so only the tumbler shows. Do not say or show anything while your child sniffs, so you give no clue.

flow.do: 1. Tie the dupatta gently over your child's eyes. 2. Check that they cannot see. 3. Tell them they will not touch the shirts.
flow.say: I am covering your eyes, so your eyes cannot help. Keep your hands in your lap, so your fingers cannot help either. Only your nose can work now.
flow.kid: Your eyes are covered. Keep your hands in your lap. Only your nose works now.

ask.q: Why do we cover your eyes?
good: So I cannot see whose shirt it is.
So the test is fair.

flow.do: 1. Hold one tumbler under your child's nose for a few slow sniffs. 2. Ask whose shirt it is. 3. Write the guess next to that tumbler's place. 4. Do every tumbler. Between tumblers, let your child sniff the inside of their own elbow.
flow.say: Take three slow sniffs. Whose shirt is this? It is fine to say 'I don't know' or 'nobody'.
flow.kid: Sniff slowly, three times. Whose shirt is it? You can say 'I don't know'.

ask.q: What does this one smell like?
good: Like hair oil and someone I know.
Like nothing, maybe it is the clean one.

flow.parent: Sniffing their own elbow between tumblers clears the nose a little. Smells are faint, so keep the tumbler close and give your child time.

flow.do: 1. Take the dupatta off. 2. Mix the tumblers again while your child turns away. 3. Cover the eyes again and do round 2. 4. Write the second guesses.
flow.say: Now we do it all again in a new order. One right guess could be luck. Two right guesses is a real clue.
flow.kid: Let's do it again in a new order. Two right guesses is not luck.
flow.parent: Keep the chits under the tumblers as you mix them.

flow.do: 1. Take off the dupatta. 2. Lift each tumbler and read the chit together. 3. Your child puts a tick on the results for each right guess.
flow.say: Let's look under the tumblers. Whose shirts did you know both times? Which ones were hard? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Look under each tumbler. Which ones did you get right? Which were hard?

ask.q: Which shirt was hardest to know, and why?
good: The clean shirt, because it smelled of nothing.
A shirt from someone I do not sit close to.

flow.parent: Often a child gets at least one person right both times, usually someone close. If your child got none right, that is a real result too. Smells on a shirt are faint. Try again with shirts worn for two nights, or let a grown-up be the sniffer. Wash the shirts afterwards.

check.q: What did you use to find whose shirt it was?
check.why: Your eyes were covered and your hands were in your lap, so only your nose could work. Right or wrong, the guesses came from your nose.

experiments.title: Pass the Smell: how far does it go along a line of hands?
experiments.context: In this experiment, one person rubs a crushed clove of garlic on their palm. Then everyone shakes hands down a line. Who still smells of garlic at the end? A smell is made of tiny bits too small to see, like microbes, and this shows how such tiny bits can pass from person to person.
experiments.question: If one person has garlic on their hand, and we shake hands down a line, how far does the smell go?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Will the last person in the line smell of garlic? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Everyone washes and dries their hands first, so they start the same. Everyone shakes hands the same way, for the count of three. Everyone smells their own palm the same way.
results_table: Garlic smell: strong, a little, or none?

materials.item: one clove of garlic
a steel spoon to crush it
soap and water
2 or more people. If you are only two, also a clean steel spoon and a clean cotton cloth

experiments.safety: Only a grown-up crushes the garlic and rubs it on a palm, for a few seconds. Keep garlic away from eyes. If the skin stings, wash at once. Everyone washes their hands with soap at the end.

schedule.what: Wash hands. Rub garlic on one palm. Pass the smell down the line. Smell each one and record.

experiments.record: Draw the line of people, and the spoon and cloth if you used them. Colour each hand: dark green for a strong smell, light green for a little, no colour for none.

setup.art: A woman pressing a peeled garlic clove under the back of a steel spoon on a chopping board.
setup.caption: 1. Crush a garlic clove. The first person rubs it on their palm.

setup.art: A line of four family members shaking hands one after another, a grandmother at the start and a small boy at the end.
setup.caption: 2. Shake hands down the line, one after another.

setup.art: A small boy sniffing his own palm with a puzzled face, while the others sniff theirs.
setup.caption: 3. Everyone smells their own palm. Who smells of garlic?

flow.do: 1. Everyone washes hands with soap and dries them. 2. Stand in a line. If you are only two, the line is: grown-up, child, steel spoon, cotton cloth. 3. Ask for a guess.
flow.say: A grown-up will put garlic on one hand. Then we pass it down the line. Will the last one in the line smell of garlic? Why?
flow.kid: One person gets garlic on their hand. We shake hands down the line. Will the last person smell of garlic? Why?

ask.q: Will the last person smell of garlic?
good: Yes, it will pass along.
No, it will be used up by then.

flow.do: 1. The grown-up stands first in the line. 2. The grown-up crushes the garlic clove with the back of the spoon. 3. The grown-up rubs it on one palm for a few seconds.
flow.say: Smell the garlic. Now the first person rubs it on their palm.
flow.kid: Smell the garlic. The first person rubs it on their palm.
flow.parent: A grown-up crushes the garlic. Throw the clove in the cooking afterwards.

flow.do: 1. The first person shakes hands with the second, for a count of three. 2. The second shakes with the third. 3. Go to the end of the line. If you are only two: after the handshake, your child holds the spoon in the hand for a count of three. Then the spoon is pressed on the cloth for a count of three.
flow.say: Shake hands, one, two, three. Now pass it on to the next person.
flow.kid: Shake hands. Count one, two, three. Pass it on.
flow.parent: Use the same hand each time. With only two people, the spoon and cloth are the end of the line. Their smell may be very faint, and that is a result too.

flow.do: 1. Everyone sniffs their own palm, then the spoon and the cloth if you used them. 2. Each says strong, a little, or none. 3. Your child records it.
flow.say: Sniff each hand in the line. Is the garlic smell strong, a little, or none? Which has the most? Which has the least?
flow.kid: Sniff each one. Strong, a little, or none?

ask.q: Why did the smell get weaker down the line?
good: Each hand got a little less than the hand before.
Some stayed on each hand.

flow.parent: Usually the first two in the line smell clearly of garlic and the end of the line smells faintly or not at all.

check.why: The first person rubbed the garlic on. Each handshake passed on only a little, so the smell got weaker down the line.

flow.do: 1. Everyone washes hands with soap. 2. Talk about microbes.
flow.say: The garlic smell passed from hand to hand. Microbes on our skin are too small to see, and they pass from hand to hand too. People who live together pass them to each other every day.
flow.kid: Tiny microbes pass from hand to hand too. Now wash with soap!

activities.title: My Home Picture: who lives with me, and who lives far away
activities.context: In this activity your child draws everyone who lives in the home on one side of a page. On the other side, they draw family who live far away, with a line to show how they keep in touch.

materials.item: a sheet of paper folded in half
crayons or colour pencils

schedule.what: Fold a page. Draw the people at home on one side and family far away on the other.

activities.record: The folded drawing, with a name under each person.

setup.art: A sheet of paper folded down the middle, with a crayon drawing of a house on the left half and a bus and a phone on the right half.
setup.caption: 1. Fold a page. Draw your home on one side.

setup.art: A child's crayon drawing of five stick people inside a house on the left, and two stick people far away on the right, joined by a dotted line to a phone.
setup.caption: 2. Draw who lives with you. Draw family far away on the other side.

flow.do: 1. Fold the page in half. 2. On the left half, your child draws a big house.
flow.say: Let's draw your family. Who lives in our home with you?
flow.kid: Draw a big house on this side. Who lives here with you?

flow.do: 1. Your child draws each person who lives in the home, inside the house. 2. You write each name under the drawing.
flow.say: Draw each person who sleeps in our home. Who looks after you when you are sick?
flow.kid: Draw everyone who lives here. Draw pets too, if you have any.

ask.q: Who looks after you when you are sick?
good: My mother and my grandmother.
My father makes me rasam.

flow.parent: Let your child decide who to include. A house help, a pet or a plant may appear. Ask about them warmly.

flow.do: 1. On the right half, your child draws family who live somewhere else. 2. Draw a line from each one to how you keep in touch: a phone, a bus, a train or a letter.
flow.say: Who is in our family but lives far away? How do we talk to them?
flow.kid: Draw family who live far away. How do you talk to them?

ask.q: Is someone far away still part of your family?
good: Yes, my aunt is my family even far away.
Yes, because we call her.

flow.do: 1. Look at the whole page together.
flow.say: Look at your family. Some are near and some are far. All of them are your family.
flow.kid: Look! Your family, near and far.

activities.title: Families of Many Kinds: listen and match
activities.context: In this activity you read out six short family stories. For each one, your child says who looks after the child in that family, and whether that family is like their own.

materials.item: two bowls and a handful of dry rajma, chana or pebbles
the six family stories, read out from the steps

schedule.what: Read six family stories. For each, say who looks after the child. Drop a bean in the 'like mine' or 'not like mine' bowl.

activities.record: Count the beans in each bowl. Draw one family from the list that is not like yours.

setup.art: A mother reading from a phone to a girl sitting cross-legged beside two steel bowls and a small heap of red rajma beans.
setup.caption: 1. Listen to each family story.

setup.art: A child's hand dropping one red rajma bean into one of two steel bowls, one labelled with a smiling face and one with a question mark.
setup.caption: 2. Drop a bean in 'like my family' or 'not like my family'.

flow.do: 1. Put the two bowls in front of your child. 2. Say which bowl is 'like my family' and which is 'not like my family'.
flow.say: I will read about six families. Listen for who looks after the child.
flow.kid: Listen to six families. Who looks after the child?

flow.do: 1. Read each family slowly. 2. After each, ask who looks after the child. 3. Your child drops a bean in one bowl.
flow.say: Family 1: Meenakshi lives in Madurai with her Paati, Thatha, Amma, Appa, aunt, uncle and two cousins. Family 2: Joyita lives in Kolkata with just her Baba. Family 3: Kayal was adopted by Revathi in Chennai. Family 4: Tenzin lives in Gangtok with her mother and her grandmother. Family 5: Lakshmi lives in Mysuru with her Amma. Her Appa works in another city and comes home each month. Family 6: Farhan lives in Pune with his two Phuphis, his aunts, who raise him.
flow.kid: Listen to each family. Who looks after the child? Is that family like yours?

ask.q: In Joyita's family, who looks after Joyita?
good: Her Baba.
Her father.

ask.q: Is Kayal's family a real family?
good: Yes, Revathi is her mother.
Yes, because they love each other.

flow.parent: Read one family at a time and wait for an answer before the next. There are no wrong bowls: the bowls show how your child sees their own family.

flow.do: 1. Count the beans in each bowl together.
flow.say: How many families are like ours? How many are different? Every one of them is a real family.
flow.kid: Count the beans in each bowl. Every one is a real family.

check.q: Which of these is a real family?
options: Only a mother, a father and children
Every one of the six families
check.why: Each of the six families has grown-ups who look after a child. Families come in many kinds, and every kind is a real family.

activities.title: Elephant Family Walk
activities.context: In this moving activity, your family walks around the home like a family of Asian elephants. An older female leads. The young ones walk in the middle, where they are safest.

materials.item: a clear path around the room or the flat

schedule.what: Walk round the home as an elephant family, with the oldest grown-up in front and the young in the middle.

activities.record: Draw your elephant family walk, with the leader at the front.

setup.art: The oldest grown-up leading a line of family members around a living room, each person holding the back of the person in front like an elephant holding a tail with a trunk.
setup.caption: 1. The oldest grown-up leads. Everyone holds on to the person in front.

setup.art: A family walking in a slow circle, with a small boy safely in the middle and grown-ups around him.
setup.caption: 2. The youngest walk in the middle, where they are safe.

flow.do: 1. Explain the elephant family. 2. Choose the oldest grown-up at home to be the leader.
flow.say: Asian elephants live in families of mothers, daughters, aunts and young ones. Often an older female leads the way to water. In our game, the oldest grown-up is the leader. She or he leads!
flow.kid: Elephant families stay together. An older female often leads. In our game, the oldest grown-up leads.
flow.parent: This is true of Asian elephants in India. T. N. C. Vidya and her team in Bengaluru study elephant families in Nagarahole forest. Grown-up male elephants leave their family and mostly live alone or in small groups.

flow.do: 1. Everyone lines up behind the leader. 2. Each person holds the back of the shirt of the person in front, like a trunk holding a tail. 3. Walk slowly round the home.
flow.say: Hold on, like a baby elephant holding their mother's tail with their trunk. Walk slowly. Our leader is taking us to the river!
flow.kid: Hold on to the person in front. Walk slowly behind the leader.
flow.parent: This is only a game. Baby elephants walk close beside their mothers.

flow.do: 1. The leader calls 'Tiger!' 2. The grown-ups stand close around the youngest child, arms out like a wall. If there is only one grown-up, stand close to your child, arms out. 3. Then walk on.
flow.say: Tiger! Quick, the young ones go in the middle. The grown-ups stand around them. Why do you think elephants do this?
flow.kid: Tiger! The little ones go in the middle. Why?

ask.q: Why do the young ones go in the middle?
good: So the tiger cannot reach them.
The big elephants keep them safe.

flow.parent: Elephant families do gather around their calves when there is danger.

activities.title: Who Else Lives in Our Home? A hunt for other living beings
activities.context: People are not the only ones who live in a home. In this hunt your child looks for other living beings that share your home: ants, a lizard, a potted plant, a crow at the window, and microbes in the curd.

materials.item: paper and a pencil
a torch, if you have one
a bowl of curd

schedule.what: Walk round the home and list every living being you find besides people.

activities.record: A list with a little drawing for each living being found, and where.

setup.art: A girl kneeling on a kitchen floor with a torch, looking at a line of tiny ants walking along the edge of the wall.
setup.caption: 1. Look in corners, near the kitchen and at the windows.

setup.art: A child's list on paper with small drawings: ants, a house lizard, a tulsi plant in a pot, a crow, and a bowl of curd.
setup.caption: 2. Draw each living being you find, and where.

flow.do: 1. Give your child the paper and pencil.
flow.say: Our family is not the only family living here. Let's find who else lives in our home.
flow.kid: Who else lives in our home? Let's look!

flow.do: 1. Walk round the home together. 2. Look near the kitchen, in corners, behind the fridge with the torch, on the walls at night, and at the windows. 3. Your child draws each living being found.
flow.say: Look near the kitchen floor. Are there ants? Look up at the wall. Is there a lizard? Is there a plant at the window?
flow.kid: Look on the floor, up the walls and at the window. Draw what you find.

ask.q: What other living beings share our home?
good: Ants in the kitchen.
A lizard on the wall.
Our tulsi plant.

flow.parent: Ants and a potted plant are found in most homes. A house lizard, a spider or a crow at the window are common too. Do not touch any of them.

flow.do: 1. Show the bowl of curd. 2. Explain that curd is full of living microbes.
flow.say: This curd is full of living microbes, too small to see. They turned the milk into curd. And millions of microbes live on our skin too. So how many living beings live in our home?
flow.kid: Curd is full of tiny living microbes. So are we! How many living beings live here?

ask.q: Is our home only for people?
good: No, ants and the lizard live here too.
No, microbes live everywhere.

projects.title: Who Looked After Me as a Baby? A three-day memory book
projects.context: In this project your child asks a family member each day about when they were a baby. Who fed them? Who sang to them? Who held them at night? They make one page a day.

materials.item: 4 sheets of paper (3 pages and a cover), stapled or tied with thread into a little book
crayons
a baby photo of your child, on a phone or printed, if you have one

schedule.what: Look at a baby photo. Ask a grown-up: what did I eat as a baby? Draw it.
Ask a grown-up: what song did someone sing to me? Sing it together and draw it.
Ask a grown-up, or call a relative who lives far away: who held me at night? Draw it and finish the cover.

projects.record: A three-page memory book, with a drawing and a sentence on each page, written by a grown-up.

setup.art: A girl showing her grandmother a baby photo on a phone, both laughing.
setup.caption: 1. Each day, ask one family member about when you were a baby.

setup.art: A small handmade book of three pages tied with red thread, open to a crayon drawing of a woman rocking a baby.
setup.caption: 2. Draw one page each day.

flow.do: 1. Look at a baby photo together. 2. Your child asks one person: what did I eat when I was a baby? 3. Your child draws it. 4. Write the answer under the drawing.
flow.say: Look, this is you as a baby! You could not walk or talk. Who fed you? Ask a grown-up what you ate.
flow.kid: Look, that is you as a baby! Ask: what did I eat? Draw it.

ask.q: What did you eat as a baby?
good: Milk, then ragi porridge.
Mashed rice and dal.

flow.parent: If your child joined the family later, ask about the first days together instead.

flow.do: 1. On day two, your child asks another person: what song did someone sing to me? 2. Sing it together. 3. Draw it.
flow.say: Who sang you to sleep? Ask a grown-up. Can they sing it now?
flow.kid: Ask: who sang to me? Sing it together. Draw it.

flow.do: 1. On day three, ask a grown-up, or call a relative far away: who held me at night? 2. Draw it. 3. Make a cover. A grown-up writes your name on it.
flow.say: When you were a baby, many people looked after you. Who held you when you cried at night? Ask a grown-up, or call a relative far away and ask.
flow.kid: Ask: who held me when I cried? Draw it. Make a cover.

ask.q: How many people looked after you as a baby?
good: Lots, my mother, my father and my grandmother.
Everyone in my family.

flow.parent: A baby needs many hands. The book shows your child how many people made sure they were fed, held and safe.

challenges.title: Make My Family Picture Stand Up
challenges.context: This is a building challenge. Take the family drawing you made in the My Home Picture activity, or draw one now. Can you make it stand up on a shelf by itself?
challenges.problem: Make your family drawing stand up on a table by itself, without leaning on a wall, for as long as you count to 20.
constraints: Use only paper, old cardboard, a small box, a lump of atta dough, tape or glue.
The picture must face the front so everyone can see it.
It must not lean on the wall or on anything else.
materials: a small box or a lump of atta dough, if you want to try them
general: Fold a strip of cardboard into a triangle and tape it to the back of the picture, like a photo frame.
Glue the picture on thick cardboard. Fold a wide strip at the bottom forward to make a flat foot.
Fold the paper into a tent shape, with the picture on one side.
creative: Cut a slot in a small box and slide the picture into the slot.
Roll two paper tubes and tape them behind the picture like legs.
Stand the picture in a lump of atta dough on a small plate.
challenges.your_turn: Now make a stand for a picture of a family who lives far away, so they can be on the shelf too.

setup.art: A child's crayon drawing of a family lying flat on a table, with a strip of cardboard, tape and safety scissors beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Start with your drawing, cardboard and tape.

setup.art: The family drawing standing upright on a shelf, held by a folded cardboard triangle taped to its back.
setup.caption: 2. Build a stand. Count to 20 to test it.

flow.do: 1. Put the drawing flat on the table. 2. Ask how to make it stand.
flow.say: Your family picture is lying down. How can we make it stand up by itself? What do you think will work?
flow.kid: Your picture is lying down. How can it stand up by itself?

ask.q: How could you make it stand?
good: Put something behind it.
Fold the bottom.

flow.do: 1. Your child tries one idea with cardboard, paper and tape. 2. Stand it on the table. 3. Count to 20 together.
flow.say: Try your idea. Stand it up and let go. Let's count to 20. Did it stay up?
flow.kid: Try your idea. Let go. Count to 20!
flow.parent: Help with cutting cardboard. If it falls, ask which way it fell, and what could stop it falling that way.

flow.do: 1. If it fell, try a second idea. 2. Put the picture on a shelf where everyone can see it.
flow.say: What made it stay up? Where shall we put our family?
flow.kid: What made it stand? Put your family on the shelf!

ask.q: What made the stand work?
good: The triangle at the back held it.
A wide foot stopped it falling.

videos.title: How your nose works, for children
videos.why: Shows how tiny bits of a thing float into the nose, and how the nose tells smells apart.
videos.check: Found by search: "How Your Nose Works? - The Dr. Binocs Show | Best Learning Videos For Kids | Peekaboo Kidz" by Peekaboo Kidz, 6 minutes. A parent may preview it.

videos.title: What makes Indian elephants special
videos.why: Shows real Indian (Asian) elephants and what is special about them, as a start for talking about elephant families.
videos.check: Found by search: "What Makes Indian Elephants So Special? | Asia Fun Facts | BBC Earth Kids" by BBC Earth Kids, 3 minutes. A parent may preview it.

videos.title: What's inside an anthill
videos.why: Shows inside an ant nest, with the queen laying eggs and her daughters caring for the young.
videos.check: Found by search: "What's Inside An Anthill? | Insider Science" by Insider Science, 3 minutes. A parent may preview it.

items.p: Draw three things in your home that you can know by their smell alone. Ask a grown-up to write what they are.
items.a: A drawing of three things with a smell, such as tea, soap or a flower.
items.why: A strong drawing shows things the child really knows by smell, which shows that smell tells us who and what is near.

items.p: Draw a line from each family to who is in it.
pairs: Mothers, aunts and young ones, with an older female leading
A queen and her many daughters
A girl who lives with only her father
items.why: Every one of these is a family, and each kind is different.
items.art: Three pictures on the left (elephants walking, ants carrying a crumb, a father and daughter) and three groups on the right.

items.p: In the shirt test, your eyes were covered. Circle what you used to guess whose shirt it was.
items.why: Your eyes were covered, so only your nose could work.

items.p: A family must always have a mother, a father and children.
items.why: False. Some families have one parent, some have grandparents raising a child, and some have aunts. Every kind with grown-ups who care is a family.

items.p: Circle the one that is NOT a family.
opts: A grandmother and her two grandchildren
A shopkeeper and the people buying rice
An aunt, an uncle and their three children
items.why: A shopkeeper and customers meet to buy and sell. They do not belong to each other or look after each other. The others are families.

items.p: Say it to a grown-up, who writes it down. Name one kind of family that is not like yours. Why is it a real family?
items.a: For example: A family with one parent is a real family, because the grown-up looks after the child.
items.why: A strong answer names a kind of family from the unit and says it is real because the grown-ups belong to the child and look after the child.

items.p: Meenakshi lives in a big joint family in Madurai. Count all the people in this picture. Write the number.
items.why: There are Paati, Thatha, Amma, Appa, an aunt, an uncle, Meenakshi and two cousins: 9 people in all.
items.art: A joint family of nine on a veranda in Madurai: a grandmother and grandfather in the middle, two men, two women and three girls.

items.p: Kavya and Lalitha, two sisters in Kochi, are talking about families.

views.says: Your family is the people you are related to, like cousins far away.
Your family is the people who live with you and look after you.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Could both be right? Then say one good thing about the other sister's idea.
items.a: Any side, with a reason. Both can be right: many people are both related and live together.
items.why: A strong answer gives a reason, for example 'Kunjamma lives far away but she is still my family'. It also sees what is good in the other view.

items.p: Nila knows her grandmother, Ammachi, by clues. Colour the clues you see in blue. Colour the clues you smell in green.
items.why: We know our family with our eyes and with our noses. A smell clue works even in the dark.

items.p: Here is the shirt test. Draw a ring round the thing that stops the eyes from helping. Draw a cross on the thing that holds the shirt.
items.a: A ring round the dupatta over the eyes. A cross on the steel tumbler.
items.why: A strong answer finds the dupatta, which makes the test fair, and the tumbler, which hides the shirt.
items.art: A girl with a dupatta tied over her eyes, sniffing a steel tumbler that her mother holds up. Two more steel tumblers stand on the table.

items.p: Nila, a girl in Kochi, sniffs two shirts. Her mother wore one all night. The other was just washed. Which one smells of a person?
items.why: A worn shirt picks up the wearer's smell. Washing takes most of it away. That is why we used a washed shirt as the 'nobody' shirt.

items.p: Say it to a grown-up, who writes it down. In your shirt test, did you know the clean shirt? What does that tell you about a shirt nobody has worn?
items.a: For example: The clean shirt smelled of nothing much, so a worn shirt smells of the person who wore it.
items.why: A strong answer uses the clean shirt from their own test as evidence that the smell on a worn shirt comes from the person.

items.p: Microbes are too small to see. Draw what you think the microbes on your hand might look like, if you could zoom in.
items.a: Any drawing of many tiny beings on a hand.
items.why: A strong drawing shows many tiny beings on the skin. Real skin microbes are round or rod-shaped, much too small to see.

items.p: A new mother can learn her baby's smell in less than one hour.
items.why: True. In 1987, Marsha Kaitz and her team in Jerusalem found that about nine out of ten new mothers could pick out their baby's shirt by smell, after between 10 minutes and an hour together.

items.p: Put the shirt test in order. Write 1, 2, 3, 4.
items: Cover the eyes with a dupatta
Put each shirt in a tumbler
a: Put each shirt in a tumbler
Cover the eyes with a dupatta
items.why: First the shirt picks up the smell. Then it goes in the tumbler. Then the eyes are covered, and last comes the sniffing.

items.p: Draw a line from each animal to how they know their family.
pairs: Touch feelers to smell if they are from the same nest
Smells her new lamb and remembers the smell
items.why: Humans and other animals use smell to know who is near. Smell is one of the most important ways.
items.art: Two ants touching feelers, a mother sheep sniffing a lamb, and a brown dog sniffing a boy's hand at a gate.

items.p: Circle the one that is NOT a way to join a family.
items.why: People join a family by being born, by adoption or by marriage. A bus ticket only takes you somewhere.

items.p: Say it to a grown-up. Arjun, a boy of four, says, 'People cannot smell each other. Only dogs use their noses.' What would you tell him from your test?
items.a: I found some of my family by smell alone, with my eyes covered. So people do use their noses.
items.why: A strong answer uses the child's own shirt test as evidence against the idea.

items.p: Here is an elephant family walking. Draw a ring round the leader. Draw a star on the young one who is safest.
items.a: A ring round the older female at the front. A star on the calf in the middle.
items.why: An older female often leads. The young ones walk in the middle, where the grown-ups can protect them.
items.art: A line of five Asian elephants walking, with a big older female in front and a small calf between two grown-ups.

items.p: People who live together pass tiny living beings to each other. These tiny beings are called ______.
items.why: Microbes live on our skin, and pass between people who hug, hold hands and share a home.

items.p: Say it to a grown-up. In the Pass the Smell test, the garlic smell got weaker down the line. Why?
items.a: Each hand kept some of the garlic and passed on only a little. So each hand had less than the one before.
items.why: A strong answer says some of the garlic stayed on each hand, so less reached the end.

items.p: Scientists found that people in one home share many skin microbes. A grandmother goes to stay for two weeks with her daughter's family. What do you guess will happen?
opts: She will share more microbes with her daughter's family
All her microbes will go away
items.why: People who live together share more skin microbes. So she will likely share more with her daughter's family. Scientists are still finding out how long shared microbes stay.

items.p: Three people in Bengaluru talk about where body smell comes from.

views.says: Your smell comes from the food you eat, like garlic and onion.
Your smell comes from tiny microbes on your skin.
You are born with your smell. It comes from your parents.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Could more than one be right? Then say one thing another person got right.
items.a: Any side with a reason. All three are partly right: food, microbes and genes all play a part.
items.why: A strong answer sees that scientists have found all three play a part, and are still finding out how much each one does.

items.p: Draw how you would test if a grown-up at home can find YOUR shirt by smell. Show what makes it fair.
items.a: A drawing of a grown-up with covered eyes, sniffing tumblers, with the child's shirt in one of them.
items.why: A strong plan covers the eyes, uses the same tumblers, keeps hands off the shirt, and does more than one round.

items.p: The ants you see walking on the kitchen floor are all girls, and daughters of a queen in their nest.
items.why: True. The worker ants are all female. Each one is a daughter of a queen in the nest.

items.p: Circle the one that is NOT a way a smell can pass from one person to another.
items.why: Smell and microbes pass by touching and sharing things. Looking at a photo does not pass anything.

items.p: Circle the one that would make the shirt test UNFAIR.
opts: All the tumblers look the same
items.why: If a grown-up whispers the answer, your nose is not doing the work. The other three keep the test fair.

items.p: Draw a line from each person to how they joined their family.
pairs: Baby Kayal and her mother Revathi
Nila and her little brother Arjun
items.why: People join families in different ways. Each way makes a real family.

items.p: Say it to a grown-up. Three tulsi plants grow side by side in one pot on the window. Are they a family? Why or why not?
items.a: For example: Yes, they live together and share the same soil and water. Or: Maybe, if they came from the same parent plant.
items.why: A strong answer gives a reason, using what a family is: belonging together, sharing a home, or coming from the same parents.

items.p: Draw an animal family you have seen near your home, like cats, crows or cows. Show who looks after the young.
items.a: A drawing of an adult animal with her young.
items.why: A strong drawing shows an adult animal close to the young ones, and says what she does for them, such as feeding or guarding.

opts: People who belong to each other and look after each other
Only people who look the same
quiz.why: A family is people who belong together and care for each other. Family members do not always look alike.

quiz.p: Tenzin lives in Gangtok with her mother and her grandmother. Is that a family?
quiz.why: Tenzin's mother and grandmother look after her. Families come in many kinds, and this is one.

quiz.p: Who often leads an Asian elephant family?
quiz.why: Elephant families are mothers, daughters, aunts and young ones. An older female often leads. Grown-up males leave.

quiz.p: In an ant nest, who lays the eggs?
quiz.why: The queen lays the eggs. The worker ants are her daughters.

quiz.p: Can people tell their family apart by smell alone?
quiz.why: Scientists found that mothers, brothers and sisters can pick out a family member's worn shirt by smell. You may have done it too.

quiz.p: Thenu, a girl in Class 1, does the shirt test once and gets one right. Why should she do it again?
opts: One right guess could be luck
Because the first time is always wrong
quiz.why: A guess can be right by luck. If she is right two times, it is more likely her nose really knows.

quiz.p: Why do we use the same kind of tumbler for every shirt?
opts: So the tumblers give no clue
quiz.why: If one tumbler looked or felt different, it could give a clue. Same tumblers make a fair test.

quiz.p: What makes much of a person's body smell?
quiz.why: Microbes on the skin feed on sweat and make much of our smell. Food, soap and genes play a part too.

quiz.p: Lakshmi and her Amma hug every day. What passes between them?
quiz.why: When people touch, some skin microbes move across. People who live together share many microbes.

quiz.p: Baby Kayal was adopted by Revathi. Will they share skin microbes?
opts: Yes, because they live close together
No, because Kayal was not born to Revathi
quiz.why: Sharing microbes comes from living together and touching, not from being born into a family. A husband and wife share many too.

applications: Doctors and nurses put a newborn baby on the mother's chest soon after birth. Skin to skin, the baby is warm and close, and starts to know the mother's smell.
Police dogs follow the smell of one person, because every person's smell is a little different.
Scientists study skin microbes to understand some skin problems and how to treat them.
Forest teams in India study elephant families to keep them safe and to know where they move.

spotted.text: A mother cat sniffing her kittens one by one on a staircase or under a parked scooter.

open_questions.q: How much of our body smell comes from genes, and how much from food and skin microbes?
open_questions.why_open: All three play a part. Scientists are still finding out how much each one matters.

open_questions.q: Do the microbes we share with our family stay on us, or come and go after each touch?
open_questions.why_open: The 2013 study found that people who live together share microbes. It could not tell how many stay for a long time.

open_questions.q: How does a new baby learn their family's smell so quickly?
open_questions.why_open: Babies seem to prefer familiar smells within days of birth, but tests do not always agree, and nobody knows exactly how this learning happens.

ask_kids: When you hug someone you love, what do they smell like?
Who in our family is first at something? Who is the earliest riser?
Who else lives in our home besides people?

maths.problem: In the shirt test, Nila guessed 5 shirts. She got 3 right. How many did she get wrong?
maths.explain: 5 shirts take away 3 right ones leaves 2. So 2 guesses were wrong.
maths.context: This is about the shirt test, where you sniffed shirts in steel tumblers with your eyes covered.
maths.why_maths: Taking away tells you how many guesses were wrong, so you can see how well your nose did.

maths.problem: Line up these family members from youngest to oldest: Appa 40, Arjun 4, Ammachi 70, Nila 6.
maths.explain: 4 is the smallest number, then 6, then 40, then 70. So Arjun is first and Ammachi is last.
maths.context: This is about the Family Line-Up game, where everyone lined up in different orders.
maths.why_maths: Putting numbers in order tells you who goes where in the line, without everyone standing up.

maths.problem: Nila's family has 5 people at home. On Sunday, 2 cousins and 1 aunt come for lunch. How many people sit down to lunch?
maths.explain: 2 cousins and 1 aunt make 3 visitors. 5 and 3 make 8. So 8 people sit down to lunch.
maths.context: This is about Nila's family from the story, when relatives come to visit.
maths.why_maths: Adding the visitors to the people at home tells you how many plates to put out.

founder: ideas/by_topic/family.md: the notebook lists family handprints, grandparents' games and handmade cards. The Class 3 unit already uses all three, so this unit builds on them in other ways: the memory book (p1) asks family members about the child's babyhood, the way the grandparents' games week asks elders about theirs.
science: Porter, R. H. and Moore, J. D. (1981). Human kin recognition by olfactory cues. Physiology and Behavior 27: 493 to 495. Siblings and mothers identified a child's worn T-shirt by smell alone.

Kaitz, M., Good, A., Rokem, A. M. and Eidelman, A. I. (1987). Mothers' recognition of their newborns by olfactory cues. Developmental Psychobiology 20: 587 to 591. About 90% of mothers recognised their newborn's smell after 10 minutes to 1 hour of contact.

Song, S. J. and others (2013). Cohabiting family members share microbiota with one another and with their dogs. eLife 2: e00458. 159 people and 36 dogs in 60 households; household members, especially couples, shared more skin microbes.
McGann, J. P. (2017). Poor human olfaction is a 19th-century myth. Science 356: eaam7263. Traces the idea to Paul Broca (1879).
Body odour comes mainly from skin bacteria breaking down sweat: for example, the review by James, A. G. and others (2013), International Journal of Cosmetic Science.

Asian elephant female social groups: work by T. N. C. Vidya's group at JNCASR, Bengaluru, on the Kabini population (Nagarahole and Bandipur), for example Nandini, Keerthipriya and Vidya (2017), Animal Behaviour.
Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956, section 12: an adopted child is the child of the adoptive parents for all purposes.

roots.context: We sniffed family shirts and passed a smell down a line of hands. Now we ask what this tells us about who we are, and what a family is.

deep_truth.truth: With your eyes covered, your nose could find some of your family. Much of each person's smell is made by microbes living on their skin. People who live together pass these microbes to each other. So everyone in one home shares tiny living beings, whether born into the family or not.
deep_truth.habit: We often say family means 'the same blood', the people you are born from. The shirt test and the microbe study show that living close together also makes people alike, even people who were not born related.
deep_truth.evidence: In the shirt test, many children find at least one family member by smell alone. In 2013, scientists found that people in one home share more skin microbes, and a husband and wife share many, though they are not related by birth.

three.who_am_i: You are a person, and also a home for millions of tiny living beings. Some of them came from the people who hug you.
three.what_is_life: Life is shared. Living beings pass to each other through every hug, every handshake and every shared tumbler.
three.what_is_this_world: The world is full of families of many kinds: elephant families, ant sisters, joint families and families of two.

roots.thread: A family begins with one person caring for another. Then more join, by birth, by marriage or by adoption. Each person brings their own smell and their own tiny beings. Living close, they share them, until the home has a smell of its own.

teachings.teaching: Only a small mind asks, 'Is this person mine, or a stranger?' For a big-hearted person, the whole world is one family: vasudhaiva kutumbakam.
teachings.link: Families come in many kinds, and people join them in many ways. Even the tiny beings on our skin move from person to person. Where a family ends is not as fixed as it looks.

teachings.source: Thich Nhat Hanh, The Heart of Understanding (1988), on interbeing
teachings.teaching: Look deeply at a sheet of paper and you can see the cloud, the rain and the tree in the paper. Nothing exists all by itself.
teachings.link: Look deeply at your own skin, and you find tiny beings that came from the people you live with. Part of each of us came from the others.

science.text: People who live in one home share more skin microbes than people from different homes.
Whether shared microbes stay on us for long, or come and go after each touch, is not yet known.

other_view.view: Family is about being born related. Genes from your parents shape your face, your body and part of your smell, and living together cannot change those genes.

practice.title: Breathe in the people you love
practice.say: Sit close to someone you love. Close your eyes. Breathe in slowly through your nose, three times. Can you smell them? Now breathe out slowly. Each breath out carries a little of you into the room. Sit quietly together for one more breath.
practice.kid: Sit close to someone you love. Close your eyes. Breathe in slowly three times. Can you smell them? Breathe out slowly.

ask: If some of your smell came from the people who hug you, is your smell only yours?
Where does your family end? Does it end at your door, or does it go further?
Baby Kayal was not born into her family. In what ways does she belong to it?

how_we_found_out.story: For a long time, many scientists thought people had a poor sense of smell. In 1879, Paul Broca, a French doctor who studied the brain, said that humans smell poorly. He said the smell part of the human brain was small next to the rest of the brain. Most people believed this for over 100 years. Then scientists began to test real noses. In 1981, Richard Porter and John Moore in the United States asked children to wear plain T-shirts. Then their brothers, sisters and mothers sniffed the shirts. They could pick out their own family member's shirt by smell alone. In 1987, Marsha Kaitz and her team in Jerusalem tested new mothers. After less than an hour with their babies, nine out of ten mothers could pick out their own baby's shirt by smell. In 2017, the brain scientist John McGann wrote that the weak human nose is a myth. The smell part of the human brain has about as many nerve cells as in many other mammals.
how_we_found_out.who: Paul Broca, a French doctor (1879); Richard Porter and John Moore in the United States (1981); Marsha Kaitz and her team at the Hebrew University in Jerusalem (1987); John McGann, a brain scientist in the United States (2017)
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: People thought humans had a weak sense of smell, much weaker than other mammals. Tests showed that people can know their own family, and a mother her new baby, by smell alone.
